That's an interesting point.

If morality is a subjective thing, then your conscience is what it is, and so long as it's satisfied your own moral sense is satisfied too. If this means your moral sense is different from others, then so be it.

If it's an objective thing, then we don't really need to follow our individual conscience at all, we can just follow the agreed-upon rules. The rules, and all their many exemptions and qualifications, will yield to study just as any science will, if they are truly objective.
Unless all well-formed consciences intrinsically follow an objective morality established by a divine creator. So morality is both objective and consciences can be followed.

If morality is objective, and if your conscience is attuned to that, then sure, you get to both follow your conscience and follow the objective rules all at once.

If they differ, and if your conscience feels fine with what you are doing, then presumably the correct approach is to ignore your conscience and follow the rules instead, while also trying to improve your conscience and get it into harmony with them. This makes perfect sense.

In practice, that seems like it's asking a lot. Here I am, at peace with my conscience, doing what I feel is moral and right... and I have to do something else instead, something that does not feel correct at all, in order to follow the objective rules described to me by someone else. I'm sure plenty of people will follow that path but you'd need a strong motivation to do so.

I suppose an easier path would be to always follow your conscience, but at the same time, to always seek to improve it. The religious folks I know will never claim to be perfect - very much the opposite, as a rule - but they will usually claim to be doing their best to improve. Being human means being flawed, after all, and we only become less flawed if we choose to be less flawed, and to do the work to get there. You don't necessarily have to switch over all at once.

Oddly enough, I think this is pretty much what everyone does, with various degrees of effort and awareness, whether they believe in an objective or subjective morality. Even atheists seek to grow and improve, and they know they are responsible for their morality because they define it for themselves.

In every case, we are guided by our feelings... a feeling of faith in a teaching or a calling, a feeling that improvement is good, or a feeling that we are not reaching our full potential. If we feel great at the end of the day then we made good choices, and if we feel ashamed or left behind, then we didn't.
Sure. I think it only works with an objective morality though, I think by definition a subjective morality has no need for improvement, right?

Well, that's up to each individual of course, but I think anyone of good character wants to improve.

I've never known anyone who has looked back upon their life and all their choices, and who has been entirely content with them. We see that we've done wrong, and it bothers us, and we try to do better. I suppose the only alternative would be a kind of smugness or complacency that would be pretty insufferable.

No matter what the root of our moral sense, I think we all handle moral questions in very much the same way, even if we understand it in entirely different terms. The obvious stuff is easy, but when faced with the tricky stuff, we typically follow the same pattern:

  • We ask people who we trust, people of good character, for their advice.

  • We look to our teachings and to our values, and to the writings that have inspired us, for guidance as well.

  • We wonder how our friends and co-workers and loved ones would evaluate our choice.

  • We apply the usual probing questions - if the situation was reversed, how would I want to be treated? What if this detail or that detail was different? What precedent does this set, and will it matter? Is this the start a slippery slope?

And we balance it all, and when we come upon the best answer that we can, then we feel good and right about our choice. And we make the occasional mistake, perhaps out of ignorance or carelessness or anger, and we feel stung by that later, and try to do better next time.

And some of us are more diligent about this than others. Some folks thrive on this stuff while others seem to embrace it only reluctantly.
Physically, mentally, emotionally, or spiritually? Also, right away, or in the long term? What about hidden acts of power, or choices which have consequences that only mature after a long while?

Not being a smartass here, but I'd say the answer to each of those questions is "yes".

If it feels good mentally, it's satisfied that part of your moral sense. If it feels good in the other ways, then it's satisfied more of it. A moral choice is rarely 100% good or bad, and our moral instinct is not a simple yes/no switch. But I still suggest that for each of these different ways for an act to be moral, we know it only by how it feels to us.
